hints: Before talking about disks, ask: when is an object allowed to count as finished, and who decides that?
Upload session plus verified parts plus one atomically published manifest. Readers only ever see a committed manifest.
Write the session record (tenant, object ID, version, expected length, part plan with checksums, expiry), then walk part retry, completion, and orphan cleanup against it.

signals: Separates upload-session metadata from immutable part bytes and publishes completion as one atomic manifest commit
Binds each part number to an expected byte range and checksum; same-content replay is safe, conflicting content is rejected
Makes completion retry return the same committed version and garbage-collects orphaned parts only after a grace period
Derives durability from a stated failure model, placement across failure domains, and a repair process rather than a replica count alone
Distinguishes deleting metadata from revoking signed URLs or cached copies that are already issued
Keeps the arithmetic honest: decimal units, raw bytes before replication or erasure-coding overhead
followups: One of two parts is missing when the client calls complete. What does the service return and why?
A client retries part 2 with a different checksum. How is the conflict detected and reported?
A region fails while repair is behind. Which acknowledged objects are still recoverable, and what evidence backs the durability claim?
A tenant deletes an object while a fifteen-minute signed URL is in flight. What can and cannot be revoked?
